title: Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.
summary: An ambiguous subcontract payment clause set a time for payment rather than transferring the owner’s insolvency risk to the subcontractors.
notes:
The following notes describe later Florida clarification and other jurisdictions’ public-policy limits. Their jurisdictional rules must not be collapsed into the holding of Peacock.

Peacock was the general contractor on a condominium project; the two subcontractors were Modern Air Conditioning and Overly Manufacturing, and the Florida Supreme Court (353 So.2d 840 (Fla. 1977)) reasoned that such clauses are presumed to fix a reasonable time for payment because small subcontractors cannot afford to bear the risk of the owner's nonpayment absent clear language shifting it.

sections.Parties: Peacock was the general contractor on a condominium project. Modern Air Conditioning performed heating and air-conditioning work, and Overly Manufacturing performed rooftop swimming-pool work under separate subcontracts.
sections.Material Facts:
Both subcontracts required final payment within thirty days after completion, the architect’s written acceptance, and full payment by the owner. The subcontractors completed their work, and no deficiencies were found. The owner, a corporation in bankruptcy, had not paid Peacock in full. Peacock therefore refused final payment to the subcontractors.

The wording could describe either a waiting period for payment or an event without which no payment would ever become due. The difference determined which party bore the risk that the owner could not pay.
sections.Procedural History: The subcontractors obtained summary judgments. The intermediate appellate court affirmed. The Florida Supreme Court considered the consolidated matters because another district had required a jury inquiry into a comparable clause. It approved the judgments and overruled the conflicting decision to the extent inconsistent with its rule.
sections.Issue: Could a court interpret the ambiguous payment provisions as a matter of law, and did payment by the owner constitute a condition of Peacock’s duty to pay?
sections.Holding: The clauses established a reasonable time for payment. They did not make the owner’s payment a condition of the subcontractors’ right to be paid.
sections.Reasoning:
The court treated the recurrent commercial relationship as suitable for judicial interpretation. Small subcontractors generally need payment for completed work and ordinarily do not agree to absorb the owner’s failure to pay. That context supported reading the ambiguous words as timing provisions.

The decision placed the burden of clear drafting on a general contractor wishing to transfer the risk. It allowed an unambiguously expressed risk transfer; it did not prohibit every pay-if-paid clause. Thus the court resolved uncertainty in the text without treating the parties’ power to arrange a different allocation as unlimited by other applicable law.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Peacock shows how transactional context and a default interpretation determine whether a clause creates a condition or simply fixes when an existing payment duty must be performed.

topics.conditions: It distinguishes a condition of payment from a time-for-payment clause.
topics.interpretation: Commercial context supplies a rule for resolving ambiguity without a jury trial in this class of transactions.
topics.risk-allocation: The general contractor bears the owner’s nonpayment risk unless the contract clearly transfers it.
topics.assent: The court infers the intended allocation from the wording and the usual subcontracting relationship.
topics.express-conditions: The question was whether 'full payment by the Owner' created an express condition precedent or merely fixed a time for payment.
topics.forfeiture: The court's presumption against reading ambiguous payment clauses as conditions rests on avoiding forfeiture of the subcontractors' earned payment.
